title: The Maghreb's Maliki school
hookLine: the Maliki school of law becomes the tradition of North and West Africa
carry: the school of medina traveled west

cards: A caliph admires a book, a collection of hadith and legal rulings by a scholar in Medina. He makes an offer: let this be the law for every land, copied out and sent to every city, so everyone follows one book.
The scholar says no. The companions of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, he answers, scattered to many lands, and the people there learned from them. Let them keep what they have.
That's how tradition tells it, and the scholar was Malik ibn Anas. His book stayed one voice among several, and yet it traveled further west than he ever did.

teach.b: Malik lived and taught in Medina, the Prophet's own city.
His book is the Muwatta, a title that can be rendered the well-trodden path, the way already smoothed by feet.

What made his method his own: alongside the Qur'an and the hadith, he gave great weight to the practice of the people of Medina, what the community there actually did, handed down from the generation that had lived beside the Prophet.
If Medina still did it, that counted as evidence. Students heard the Muwatta from Malik and carried it home. Some went west.
In Kairouan, in what is now Tunisia, scholars gathered his teaching into great law books. In al-Andalus, a student's copy of the Muwatta became the version people learned.
From there the school spread through the Maghreb, and along the trade routes across the Sahara into West Africa. Yesterday's Qadi Iyad was a Maliki judge; the Almoravids held to Maliki law closely.
One visible sign: some Malikis pray with their arms at their sides rather than folded. A Maliki is not a different kind of Muslim.

teach.h: SCHOOLS DIFFER IN METHOD, NOT FAITH.
teach.b: The schools of Sunni law, the Hanafi, the Maliki, the Shafi'i and the Hanbali, share the same Qur'an and prayers, and differ in method and detail.
Sunni scholars have long treated the four as ways of reading the same sources, not rival faiths. Shia Muslims have their own schools of law, such as the Ja'fari.
That closes this stretch on Cairo, the Maghreb and the scholars.

teach.h: THE SCHOOL OF MEDINA TRAVELED WEST.
teach.b: The school of Medina traveled west.

how: The Maliki school is followed in North and West Africa, the Muwatta of Imam Malik is still studied, and some Maliki worshippers pray with their arms at their sides.

games.q: you're Malik ibn Anas. the caliph offers to make your book the one law for every land. what do you do?
o: accept, so everyone follows one book.
refuse, and let each land keep what it learned.
ask for time to write a longer book.
games.why: tradition says he refused: the companions scattered to many lands, and the people there had learned from them.

practice: Think of the mosque nearest you, a Muslim friend or neighbor, or the country your family comes from: do you know which school of law they follow?

Then bring to mind Malik's answer to the caliph, let the people keep what they learned. If you pray, ask for respect for those who pray a little differently; if you don't, hold that picture of one path walked in many ways.

wordCard.voice: Muwatta. Malik of Medina's book of law, the well-trodden path, whose school traveled west and took root in North and West Africa. Today's word.
